Credit Card Clustering Project¶

Introduction

Credit card companies generate large volumes of transactional data that reflect customer spending behavior, credit usage patterns, and repayment habits. However, this data is often underutilized when treated as a homogeneous population.

This project applies unsupervised machine learning techniques, specifically clustering algorithms, to segment credit card users into distinct behavioral groups based on their financial activity. The goal is to uncover hidden structure in the data without predefined labels and translate these patterns into actionable customer segments.

By analyzing features such as spending frequency, transaction amounts, credit utilization, and payment behavior, the model identifies groups of users with similar financial characteristics. These clusters can then be interpreted to support strategic decisions such as targeted marketing, credit risk assessment, customer retention strategies, and product personalization.

The project follows a standard data science workflow including data preprocessing, feature engineering, scaling, dimensionality reduction, clustering model selection, and cluster interpretation.

Ultimately, the objective is not only to build a clustering model, but to derive meaningful business insights from customer behavior patterns.

Data Understanding¶

There are 8950 instances (rows) and 18 columns in the dataset.

Columns Description

  1. Cust Id: This is a unique identifier for each customer in the dataset. It carries no behavioural or predictive information and will not be included in the predictor variables.

  2. Balance: This represents the outstanding amount left on the credit card account. It ranges from 0 to 19043 and has an average value of 1564.5

  3. Balance Frequency: This measures how often the balance is updated. It ranges from 0 to 1.

  4. Purchases: This represents the total monetary value of all purchases on the credit card account. It ranges from 0 to 49040.

  5. Oneoff Purchases: This represents the total value of single-transaction purchases. A high value indicates luxury/high ticket buyers.

  6. Installments Purchases: This represents the total value of purchases paid in installments. A high value indicates a credit-dependent consunption behaviour.

  7. Cash Advance: This represents the toal amount of cash withdrawn using the credit card as some banks allow this. A high value indicates liquidity-dependent users.

  8. Purchases Frequency: This represents how often purchases occur, already scaled frrom 0 to 1.

  9. Oneoff Purchases Frequency: This represents the frequency of oneoff purchases, already scaled from 0 to 1.

  10. Purchases Installments Frequency: This represents the frequency of installment purchases.

  11. Cash Advance Frequency: This represents the frequency of cash withdrawals on the credit card.

  12. Cash Advance Trx: This represents the number of cash withdrawal transactions.

  13. Purchases Trx: This represents the number of purchase transactions.

  14. Credit Limit: This represents the maximum credit amount allowed for the customer. High amount could indicate creditworthiness.

  15. Payments: This represents the total amount paid back by the customer. A high value indicate responsible repayment behaviour.

  16. Minimum Payments: This represents the minimum required repayment amount. There are 13 nan values in this column and they will be filled with 0.

  17. Prc Full Payment: This represents the proportion of months were full balance was paid by the customer.

  18. Tenure: This represents the length of relationship with the credit card provider, in months

Correlation Heatmap Interpretation¶

The correlation heatmap helps identify which features contain similar information (are highly corrrlated) and which ones provide unique signals (have low correlation). This is important because K-Means clustering, which will be used in this project, is distance-based, so highly correlated variables can over-emphasize certain behaviors.

  1. Highly Correlated Features (Redundant Information)

Some features move closely together, meaning they describe the same behavior:

  • Purchases and Oneoff Purchases Total spending is largely driven by single large purchases. These two features carry very similar information.
  • Purchases Frequency and Installments Related Features Frequent shoppers tend to use installment payments more often, showing a link between usage frequency and credit-based spending.
  • Cash Advance and Cash Advance Trx Customers who take cash advances often do so repeatedly, not as one-time behavior.

Interpretation:

These variables overlap and represent the same underlying customer behavior. If not handled properly, they can bias the clustering model.

  1. Weakly Correlated Features (Independent Signals)

Some variables do not strongly relate to others:

  • Tenure: Customer duration is not strongly linked to spending or repayment patterns.
  • Credit Limit vs usage features Having a high credit limit does not guarantee high spending or activity.

Interpretation These features provide separate information and help define different customer types.

  1. Risk and Payment Behavior

Some relationships show financial behavior patterns:

  • Balance and Cash Advance Customers with higher balances are more likely to take cash advances, which can signal financial pressure.
  • Payments and Purchases People who spend more also pay more, but not always fully or consistently.
  • Prc Full Payment Shows how often customers fully clear their balance, separating disciplined users from those who carry debt.

Summary

The dataset contains overlapping spending features, independent behavioral features, and credit-risk-related features. If used directly, correlated variables may distort clustering results.

Decision

No features will be dropped at this stage. Instead, PCA will be used later to:

  • reduce correlation effects,
  • combine related features into components, and
  • simplify the dataset while keeping all information.

This ensures clustering is done on a cleaner and more balanced feature space.

Data Preprocessing¶

Next I drop any variable that won't be uses towards the analysis, then I scale the data to ensure the K-Means algorithm treats all variable with equal weight.

The scaling technique I use is the Robust Scaler due to it's ability to handle outliers better than the Standard Scaler.

The Robust Scaler is calculated by subtracting the median from each data point and dividing it by the IQR.

The mathematical formula for the Robust Scaler is:

$$X_{scaled} = \frac{X_i - \text{median}(X)}{IQR}$$

Where:

  • $X_i$: The individual data point.
  • $\text{median}(X)$: The 50th percentile ($Q_2$), which is less sensitive to outliers than the mean.
  • $IQR$: The Interquartile Range ($Q_3 - Q_1$), representing the middle 50% of the data.
In [8]:
from sklearn.preprocessing import RobustScaler

df.drop('cust_id', axis=1, inplace=True)

scaler = RobustScaler()

df_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(df)

Principal Component Analysis (PCA)¶

​Principal Component Analysis is a dimensionality reduction technique used to transform a large set of variables into a smaller one that still contains most of the information (variance) from the original dataset.

​Why PCA is used in this project:

  • ​Handling Multicollinearity: As seen in our correlation heatmap, several features are highly redundant. PCA creates new, uncorrelated features called Principal Components.
  • ​Reducing Noise: By focusing on the components that capture the most variance, we can filter out minor fluctuations (noise) that might confuse the clustering algorithm.
  • ​Optimizing K-Means: K-Means performs better in lower-dimensional spaces, as high dimensionality can cause all data points to appear equidistant (the "Curse of Dimensionality").

I will apply PCA to the scaled data to reduce the 17 behavioral features into a smaller subset of components. I will determine the optimal number of components by analyzing the Explained Variance Ratio, ensuring we retain at least 90-95% of the original information.

In [9]:
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

pca = PCA()
pca.fit(df_scaled)

Scree Plot Interpretation¶

Haven scaled the data and applying the PCA for dimensionality reduction, above are the scree plot and the cumulative explained variance plot.

Scree Plot Analysis (Individual Variance)

​The Scree Plot illustrates the variance captured by each individual Principal Component. ​We observe a sharp decline in explained variance after the first three components. ​A visible "elbow" or point of diminishing returns occurs around Component 7, after which the incremental information gained by adding further components becomes marginal.

​Cumulative Variance Threshold

​To quantify the trade-off between simplicity and data integrity, I analyzed the Cumulative Explained Variance:

​By selecting 7 Principal Components, we successfully capture 90% of the original dataset’s total variance.

​This represents a 60% reduction in dimensionality (from 17 to 7 features) while maintaining a high level of informational accuracy.

​Conclusion

Selecting 7 components ensures that the subsequent K-Means algorithm is not misled by redundant features or high-dimensional "noise." This curated feature space provides a robust foundation for identifying distinct customer segments based on their primary financial behaviors (e.g., high-volume spending vs. cash-advance dependency).

PCA Loadings Interpretation: Decoding the Principal Components¶

While PCA reduces dimensionality, it creates abstract components that can be difficult to interpret. By analyzing the Loadings Heatmap, we can see which original features contribute most to each Principal Component (PC). This allows us to assign "human" labels to these dimensions before feeding them into the K-Means algorithm.

Key Component Profiles:¶

  • Pc1: High-Volume Spenders (Overall Activity)

    • Strong Positive Loadings: Purchases (0.41), Oneoff_Purchases (0.54), and Minimum_Payments (0.51).
    • Interpretation: This component represents the overall scale of usage. High scores here indicate "power users" who make large, single transactions and have high balance-related activity.

  • Pc2: The "Minimum Payers" (Credit Risk)

    • Strong Negative Loading: Minimum_Payments (-0.8).
    • Interpretation: This component captures payment discipline. A high negative score suggests customers who are struggling to pay more than the bare minimum, indicating potential financial pressure or a "revolver" credit profile.

  • Pc3: Cash Advance Dependency

    • Strong Positive Loadings: Cash_Advance (0.59) and Cash_Advance_Trx (0.5).
    • Interpretation: This is a very specific behavioral signal. It separates users who primarily use their card for cash withdrawals—a high-interest, high-risk behavior—from those who use it for retail purchases.

  • Pc4: Active Account Management

    • Strong Positive Loading: Balance_Frequency (0.55).
    • Interpretation: This represents "stickiness." It identifies how consistently a customer interacts with their account balance, regardless of the dollar amount spent.

  • Pc5: Disciplined Full-Payers

    • Strong Positive Loading: Prc_Full_Payment (0.7).
    • Interpretation: This component isolates the most fiscally disciplined customers. High scores here represent "Transactors" who use the card for convenience but pay their balance in full, avoiding interest.

  • Pc6: Installment Shoppers

    • Strong Positive Loading: Installments_Purchases (0.63).
    • Interpretation: This captures a specific lifestyle choice: customers who prefer structured, recurring payments over one-off big ticket items.

  • Pc7: Customer Loyalty (Tenure)

    • Strong Positive Loading: Tenure (0.84).
    • Interpretation: This component is almost entirely driven by how long the customer has been with the bank, allowing us to distinguish long-term loyalists from new acquisitions.

Conclusion for Clustering¶

By transforming our 17 original variables into these 7 Distinct Behavioral Dimensions, I have effectively filtered out the noise. The K-Means algorithm will now group customers based on these meaningful archetypes (e.g., "Loyal Installment Shoppers" or "High-Risk Cash Advance Users") rather than redundant raw data.

K-Means Clustering Algorithm¶

The next step is to initialize the k-means clustering algorithm to cluster the decomposed data. The k-means clustering algorithm is selected because it is an efficient, distance-based unsupervised learning method that excels at partitioning data into distinct, non-overlapping subgroups.

​For this project, K-Means is specifically chosen because:

  • ​Computational Efficiency: It handles large datasets, like our credit card records, much faster than hierarchical clustering methods.
  • ​Compatibility with PCA: K-Means relies on Euclidean distance. Since PCA has already centered our data and removed multicollinearity, the "distance" between points in the 7D component space now has a much clearer behavioral meaning.
  • ​Actionable Segmentation: It forces every customer into exactly one cluster, which is ideal for creating clear-cut marketing strategies (e.g., specific campaigns for "Power Spenders" vs. "Cash-Advance Users").

​Determining the Number of Clusters (K)

​To find the optimal number of clusters, I use a two-pronged approach to ensure the segments are mathematically sound and practically useful:

  1. ​​The Elbow Method (WCSS): I plot the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares for a range of k values. We are looking for the "elbow" where the drop in WCSS slows down, indicating that adding more clusters provides diminishing returns in explaining the data's variance.
  2. ​Silhouette Score Analysis: To validate the elbow, I calculate the Silhouette Score, which measures how similar a point is to its own cluster compared to other clusters. A higher score indicates well-defined, separated segments.
In [13]:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
In [14]:
k_range = np.arange(1, 11)
wcss = []
silhouette_scores = []

for k in k_range:
    kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42)
    kmeans.fit(pca_df)
    wcss.append(kmeans.inertia_)

# 1. Calculate Silhouette Scores (Start from 2 clusters)
silhouette_avg = []
k_range_sil = range(2, 11)

for k in k_range_sil:
    kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42, n_init=10)
    labels = kmeans.fit_predict(pca_df)
    silhouette_avg.append(silhouette_score(pca_df, labels))

# 2. Plotting side-by-side
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 6))

# Plot WCSS (Elbow)
ax1.set_xlabel('Number of Clusters (K)')
ax1.set_ylabel('WCSS', color='#e74c3c', fontsize=12)
ax1.plot(range(1, 11), wcss, marker='o', color='#e74c3c', linewidth=2, label='WCSS (Elbow)')
ax1.tick_params(axis='y', labelcolor='#e74c3c')
ax1.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Create a second y-axis for Silhouette Score
ax2 = ax1.twinx()
ax2.set_ylabel('Silhouette Score', color='#2c3e50', fontsize=12)
ax2.plot(k_range_sil, silhouette_avg, marker='s', color='#2c3e50', linewidth=2, linestyle='--', label='Silhouette Score')
ax2.tick_params(axis='y', labelcolor='#2c3e50')

plt.title('Selecting Optimal K: Elbow Method vs Silhouette Score', fontsize=15, fontweight='bold')
plt.xticks(range(1, 11))

plt.tight_layout()
plt.legend(loc='best')
plt.savefig("selecting_k.png", dpi=300)
plt.show()

Determining Optimal K: A Multi-Metric Approach¶

​The selection of the number of clusters (K) is a critical decision that balances mathematical cohesion with practical business utility. To ensure the most robust segmentation, I utilized a dual-validation approach using the Elbow Method (WCSS) and Silhouette Analysis.

  1. The Elbow Method (WCSS) Analysis

​The WCSS plot shows a primary inflection point (the "Elbow") at K=4, where the rate of decrease in within-cluster variance begins to slow. In many basic analyses, K=4 would be the default choice. However, a secondary, more subtle "shelf" appears between K=7 and K=8, suggesting that further partitioning might still yield meaningful behavioral separation.

  1. Silhouette Score Validation

​To resolve the ambiguity of the Elbow plot, I analyzed the Silhouette Score, which measures cluster separation and individual point belonging.

​Interestingly, the score reaches a local minimum at K=4 and K=5, indicating that while these clusters are mathematically compact, they suffer from significant overlap and poor definition. ​The score begins a consistent upward trend after K=5, reaching a significant local maximum at K=8 (with K=7 showing nearly identical stability).

Conclusion

​While K=4 is simpler, the Silhouette Score proves it results in "muddy" clusters. Therefore, I have selected K=8 as the optimal number of clusters. This choice ensures maximum segment separation and provides the granularity necessary for developing highly targeted marketing strategies and risk profiles for the bank’s diverse customer base.

In [15]:
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=8, random_state=42, n_init=10)
kmeans.fit(pca_df)

pca_df['cluster'] = kmeans.labels_
In [16]:

sns.set_style("whitegrid")

for ax in g1.axes.flat:
    ax.axhline(0, ls='-', c='black', alpha=0.3, linewidth=1)
    sns.despine(ax=ax, left=True, bottom=True)
    ax.set_xticks(range(7))

Customer Segmentation Interpretation¶

The clustering results reveal clear behavioral differences across customers when viewed through the seven principal components derived from PCA. Instead of relying on raw variables, each cluster reflects a combination of spending level, credit usage, repayment behavior, and customer lifecycle. This makes the segmentation more meaningful and easier to connect to real-world financial behavior.

1. Cluster 0: Low Activity Users¶

Cluster 0 represents low-activity customers whose scores are close to neutral across most components. These users do not spend much, rarely use credit features like installments or cash advances, and show minimal engagement overall. Their behavior suggests either very light usage or near dormancy. From a business perspective, this group contributes little revenue and would benefit from activation strategies such as targeted offers or usage incentives.

2. Cluster 1: Balanced Users¶

Cluster 1 consists of moderately active customers with balanced behavior across spending and repayment. They use their cards regularly for purchases but do not rely heavily on risky features like cash advances or minimum-only payments. This group represents a stable middle segment—engaged but controlled. They are ideal candidates for upselling strategies such as gradual credit limit increases or personalized financial products.

3. Cluster 2: High Credit Users (Revenue + Risk)¶

Cluster 2 shows strong activity across spending, cash advances, and installment purchases. These customers rely heavily on credit both for consumption and liquidity. Their weaker alignment with full payment behavior suggests they often carry balances. This makes them a high-revenue segment due to interest generation, but also a higher-risk group that requires monitoring and potential risk controls.

4. Cluster 3: Inactive / Near-Churn Users¶

Cluster 3 is defined by extremely low scores across almost all components. These customers show little to no interaction with their credit cards and may be new users, inactive accounts, or customers who have effectively stopped using their cards. This segment highlights potential issues in onboarding or retention and should be targeted with re-engagement strategies.

5. Cluster 4: High Spenders (One-Off Dominant)¶

Cluster 4 captures customers with high overall spending, particularly driven by large one-off purchases, without strong reliance on installments or cash advances. This suggests financially stable users who use credit cards for convenience rather than necessity. These are typically high-value customers who should be targeted with premium services, rewards programs, and retention-focused strategies.

6. Cluster 5: Disciplined Users (Full Payers)¶

Cluster 5 consists of customers who show strong full-payment behavior and low exposure to risk-related features. They actively use their credit cards but consistently pay off their balances in full, avoiding interest. While they may not generate high interest revenue, they are low-risk, financially disciplined users who contribute to long-term portfolio stability.

7. Cluster 6: High-Risk Credit-Dependent Users¶

Cluster 6 represents the most financially stressed segment. These customers combine high spending with very high cash advance usage, indicating strong reliance on borrowed liquidity. Their behavior suggests financial pressure and a higher likelihood of default. This group requires strict monitoring, potential credit limit adjustments, and risk management interventions.

8. Cluster 7: Loyal Long-Term Customers¶

Cluster 7 is primarily driven by tenure rather than spending or credit behavior. These are long-standing customers with relatively stable usage patterns. Their value lies in long-term relationship potential rather than immediate profitability. Retention strategies and cross-selling opportunities are key for this segment.

Overall Conclusion¶

The clustering approach successfully segments customers into meaningful behavioral groups that go beyond simple spending levels. By using PCA, the model captures deeper patterns in how customers interact with credit—ranging from disciplined usage to high-risk dependency. This segmentation provides a strong foundation for both targeted marketing strategies and effective risk management.

Conclusion and Summary of Findings¶

This project set out to segment credit card customers based on their financial behavior using unsupervised machine learning. By combining feature engineering, scaling, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and K-Means clustering, the analysis moved beyond raw transactional data to uncover structured behavioral patterns within the customer base.

A key outcome of the analysis is that customer behavior is not one-dimensional. Instead, it is driven by multiple underlying factors including spending intensity, credit dependency, repayment discipline, and account tenure. PCA was instrumental in transforming the original variables into these distinct behavioral dimensions, reducing noise and eliminating redundancy while preserving the core information in the dataset.

The clustering results revealed clear and interpretable customer segments. These include low-activity users with minimal engagement, balanced users with stable spending habits, high-value customers who drive significant transaction volume, and credit-dependent users who rely heavily on cash advances and installment payments. Additionally, the segmentation identified financially disciplined users who consistently pay off their balances, as well as high-risk customers who show signs of financial stress and potential default. A separate group of long-tenured customers was also observed, highlighting the importance of lifecycle-based segmentation alongside behavioral patterns.

From a business perspective, these findings demonstrate that different customer groups require different strategies. High-value customers are best targeted with retention and rewards programs, while inactive users need engagement and activation efforts. Credit-dependent and high-risk segments require closer monitoring and risk controls, whereas disciplined users contribute to portfolio stability despite generating less interest revenue. This reinforces the importance of segmentation as a tool for both revenue optimization and risk management.

Overall, the project shows that clustering, when combined with proper preprocessing and dimensionality reduction, can effectively uncover meaningful customer segments in financial data. The resulting insights provide a practical foundation for decision-making in areas such as marketing, customer retention, credit policy, and risk assessment.
